newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM's support up since election called - survey.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM's support up since election called - survey.

text.p: The popularity of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's government rose slightly after he dissolved Japan's parliament last week for snap elections, according to a poll published on Wednesday.
The poll showed 52.3 percent of those surveyed approved of Hashimoto's cabinet, up 5.3 percentage points from the previous survey held in July.
Hashimoto dissolved the Lower House of parliament last Friday and called general elections for October 20.
More than 30 percent of those who said they approve of the Hashimoto administration said they feel they have no alternative, while 18.8 percent said the reason was that they trusted Hashimoto.
The survey, by Kyodo news agency, polled 3,000 people over the weekend, getting a response rate of 66.9 percent.

Among those disapproving of Hashimoto's administration, 14.0 percent said they had no expectations of administrative reform, 13.7 percent said they expected little from the government's economic policy and 12.4 percent said they did not trust Hashimoto.

By political grouping, Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) -- the largest of the three parties in Japan's ruling coalition -- had the highest support rate, up 3.5 percentage points from July at 38.5 percent.

The fledgling Democratic Party of Japan, formed only last week, enjoyed a support rate of 12.4 percent. It came in a close third, right on the heels of the main opposition Shinshinto, which had a 12.8 percent support rate, up 2.6 points from the previous poll.
The Democratic Party, consisting mainly of defectors from the other two coalition parties, boasts Health Minister Naoto Kan as one of its leaders.
Kan achieved hero status this year when he revealed Health Ministry complicity in a decades-old scandal in which HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, was spread through untreated blood products.

The proportion of those without preference for any mainstream political party fell to 18.1 percent from 38.1 percent in July, due partly to the birth of the Democratic Party as a new force in Japanese politics, Kyodo said.

The Social Democratic Party (SDP), currently co-led by former prime minister Tomiichi Murayama and former Lower House Speaker Takako Doi, won a 6.8 percent support rate, up from 4.7 percent in July. The Japan Communist Party's support rate rose 0.4 percentage point to 4.1 percent.
